prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BE" (ticker BE), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BE", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Bloom Energy Corporation
result.industry: Solid oxide fuel cell on-site power generation
markets: On-site (behind-the-meter) power for AI and cloud data centers
Commercial and industrial on-site power and microgrids (semiconductor fabs, hospitals, retailers, campuses)
Long-term service and electricity sales for its installed fleet

mission.statement: To make clean, reliable energy affordable for everyone in the world.
mission.plain: Bloom wants anyone, anywhere to be able to get power that is clean, always on and cheap enough to use.

about.plain: Bloom Energy builds big boxes called fuel cells that make electricity right where it is needed, without burning anything. Natural gas, biogas or hydrogen goes in, and a chemical reaction inside ceramic plates makes power, a bit like a giant battery that never runs out as long as fuel keeps coming. Big companies put these boxes next to their buildings so they do not have to wait years for a power-line connection. Today its biggest buyers are companies building AI data centers, like Oracle.
about.customers: Big companies and utilities, especially data-center builders such as Oracle, Equinix, CoreWeave and AEP, plus factories, hospitals and stores.
about.everyday: When you ask an AI chatbot a question, the data center answering it may be running on electricity from Bloom fuel cells parked outside.

money.plain: selling Bloom Energy Server power boxes ($1,531.3M in FY2025)
maintaining and replacing parts in installed fuel cells under long contracts ($228.3M)
setting up the systems at customer sites ($204.1M)
selling power from Bloom-owned systems under long-term contracts ($60.4M)
gigawatt-scale deals such as Oracle's up to 2.8 GW (April 2026) and a Brookfield partnership announced at $5B in Oct 2025
solid oxide machines that split water into hydrogen using electricity and heat

result.summary: Bloom has a real but young advantage: 20+ years of solid oxide fuel cell know-how, an installed base of about 1.4 GW at over 1,000 sites (Reuters, Oct 2025), and US factories that can deliver power in weeks rather than the years a grid connection takes. The AI power shortage has turned that speed into pricing power (gross margin up from 14.8% in 2023 to 33.8% in Q3 2026), but gas turbines, reciprocating engines and other fuel cell makers compete for the same demand and the edge depends on continued cost and reliability leadership.

pricingPower.evidence: As AI data-center demand surged, GAAP gross margin rose from 14.8% (FY2023) to 29.0% (FY2025) and 33.8% in Q3 2026 while revenue grew 138% year over year; but large customers like Oracle buy under negotiated master agreements, and turbine and engine makers offer alternatives, so pricing is strong mainly while grid power is scarce.

moats.evidence: Bloom is the best-known stationary fuel cell brand among data-center and utility buyers, backed by a large patent portfolio on solid oxide cells, and was added to the S&P 500 in 2026.

Installed systems come with long-term service contracts (service revenue $228.3M in FY2025) and customers like Equinix (100+ MW) and Oracle keep reordering, but new capacity can be bought from rivals project by project.
One customer's use of Bloom servers does not make the product more valuable to another.

Bloom is by far the largest solid oxide fuel cell maker (FY2025 revenue $2,024M vs FuelCell Energy's $158M) and planned to double factory capacity to 2 GW a year by end-2026, driving costs down; versus mass-produced gas turbines and engines its cost per kW is not clearly lower.
The on-site power market is large and open to many suppliers, so there is no natural limit on competitors.

Its modular, fast-to-deploy (an Oracle system delivered in 55 days in 2025) on-site power model is awkward for utilities and turbine makers whose businesses rely on large centralized plants and multi-year grid queues.
More than two decades of making ceramic solid oxide cells reliably at volume, a problem that has defeated many rivals, is embedded in its Fremont/Newark manufacturing processes.
It relies on materials like scandium and on supply-chain partners rather than exclusive assets, though management says it has secured sufficient non-China scandium supply.

customers.evidence: Repeat and expanding orders from marquee customers, e.g. Oracle expanded to up to 2.8 GW in April 2026 after earlier deployments and Equinix has over 100 MW deployed; no published NPS or retention statistics.

talent.evidence: Employs more than 2,000 people with a long-tenured founder-led team and stated values 'BE Bold, BE Inspired, BE Agile'; no notable top-employer rankings found.

product.evidence: Its solid oxide Energy Server is the leading commercial SOFC at scale; the company says it uses 15-20% less fuel than combustion turbines for the same output and can be deployed in weeks, which won it gigawatt-scale AI data-center deals.

competitors.name: GE Vernova
competitors.note: Gas turbines (including aeroderivatives) competing to power data centers on-site and via utilities.

competitors.name: Caterpillar (Solar Turbines, gas gensets)
competitors.note: Gas reciprocating engines and Solar Turbines units for behind-the-meter data-center power.

competitors.name: Siemens Energy
competitors.note: Gas turbines and grid equipment for large data-center and utility projects.

competitors.name: Cummins
competitors.note: Gas generators and backup power; also Accelera electrolyzers versus Bloom's hydrogen business.

competitors.name: Wartsila
competitors.note: Gas engine power plants for on-site and grid-balancing power.

competitors.name: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries
competitors.note: Gas turbines and SOFC development for power generation.

competitors.name: FuelCell Energy
competitors.note: Carbonate and solid oxide stationary fuel cells, now targeting data centers.

competitors.name: Doosan Fuel Cell
competitors.note: Phosphoric-acid and SOFC stationary fuel cells, main rival in South Korea.

competitors.name: Plug Power
competitors.note: PEM fuel cells and electrolyzers; overlaps mainly in hydrogen.

competitors.name: Ballard Power Systems
competitors.note: PEM fuel cells, mostly for mobility, some stationary backup.

competitors.name: Ceres Power
competitors.note: Licenses solid oxide fuel cell and electrolyzer technology to manufacturers such as Doosan and Delta.

competitors.name: Generac
competitors.note: Large gas and diesel generators for data-center and commercial backup and prime power.

competitors.name: Tesla (Megapack)
competitors.note: Battery storage paired with solar as an alternative on-site energy solution.

marketShare.market: Stationary fuel cell power (no reliable published shares found; Bloom is widely regarded as the largest supplier outside Korea/Japan)

threats: Fast-growing gas turbine and reciprocating-engine supply (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Caterpillar, Wartsila) could ease the on-site power shortage that currently favours Bloom's speed
Customer concentration in a few hyperscalers and partners (Oracle, Brookfield, AEP) and the risk that AI data-center capex slows
Natural gas price spikes or tighter emissions rules for gas-fired on-site generation
Grid build-out and interconnection reform reducing the need for behind-the-meter power
Execution risk scaling factories to 2 GW+ a year and supply of materials such as scandium
Large convertible debt ($2.47B recourse debt) and dilution from convertibles and warrants (diluted shares 324.3M vs 294.8M basic in Q3 2026)

ceo.name: KR Sridhar
ceo.background: Mechanical engineer (PhD, University of Illinois), former University of Arizona aerospace and mechanical engineering professor and NASA advisor whose Mars oxygen-generation work became Bloom's solid oxide technology

c1.evidence: Bloom is the leading solid oxide fuel cell company in the fast-emerging on-site power-for-AI industry, with revenue up 138% year over year to $1,235.8M in Q3 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Bloom for speed (an Oracle system online in 55 days versus years for a grid hookup), fuel efficiency and modularity; its 20 years of SOFC know-how is hard to copy, but gas turbines and engines remain credible alternatives.

c3.evidence: Bloom is the default name in stationary fuel cells for data-center and utility buyers and joined the S&P 500 in 2026, but most ordinary people have never heard of it.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to make clean, reliable energy affordable for everyone in the world' has guided founder KR Sridhar for over 20 years through years of losses; succeeding would matter for energy access and AI growth.

c6.evidence: "fuel cells, AI power, volatile stock, clean energy" - investors and buyers now see it as a key AI-power supplier, though long losses and past controversies over emissions claims make the impression mixed but increasingly positive.

c7.evidence: AI data centers are creating a multi-gigawatt power shortage; management cited visibility on about 25 GW of prospective deployments in 2026.

c8.evidence: The same solid oxide platform extends to hydrogen electrolyzers, carbon capture, utilities (AEP) and international markets such as Korea and India.

m1.evidence: Sridhar long argued that on-site generation would replace the centralized grid for critical loads, a view the AI power crunch has validated ('building the electricity platform for the digital era').

m2.evidence: Sridhar founded the company in 2001 and has run it as CEO for over two decades, persisting through many unprofitable years.

m4.evidence: No clear public evidence either way on servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: The board credits leadership with a 'culture of innovation and drive' and values 'BE Bold, BE Inspired, BE Agile', and new products (electrolyzer, higher-density servers) keep coming, but there are few outside accounts of the culture.

m6.evidence: Sridhar is a mechanical/aerospace engineer and former professor who led NASA-related solid oxide research that became Bloom's core technology.

m7.evidence: He has pursued clean, affordable energy for decades, though the company has faced criticism over its emissions claims and early-years accounting.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Sridhar giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Known for evangelical pitches (the 2010 '60 Minutes' Bloom Box launch), but not a widely recognized public personality.

m9.evidence: After a decade of losses he has delivered rapid growth (revenue $794M in 2020 to $2,024M in 2025 and 2026 guidance of $4.4-4.6B) and profitability in 2026, but the record before 2024 was weak.

m10.evidence: No well-known evidence of notable frugality.

c10.evidence: Its power keeps data centers, hospitals and factories running worldwide, but it serves businesses rather than directly improving the lives of billions.

p2.evidence: Making ceramic solid oxide fuel cells that run reliably for years at 800 degrees Celsius at gigawatt scale is very hard, and reliable clean power is vital for AI and the grid.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 20.9% (FY2020) to 29.0% (FY2025) and operating margin from -10.2% to +3.6%, but with a dip to 12.4% gross margin in FY2022.

f3.evidence: At Sept 30, 2026, debt of $2,476.4M roughly equals cash of $2,486.7M and equity is positive at $1,963.1M, but debt is high relative to its still-short history of positive cash flow.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from -$80.8M (FY2020) to +$72.8M (FY2025) and operating cash flow from -$98.8M to +$113.9M, with Q3 2026 operating income of $225.4M.

v1.evidence: Bloom's fuel cells are the best-proven choice when a data center needs clean-ish firm power fast, but for many buyers a gas turbine or grid power is an equally good or cheaper option.

v2.evidence: No appearance found in major best-employer rankings.

c5.evidence: It lets data centers and hospitals get reliable power quickly with less pollution than burning fuel; AI builders like Oracle would miss it, but others could eventually fill the gap with turbines.
